titleStmt.title: Memorandum From the President’s Assistant for National Security Affairs (McFarlane) to President Reagan

div.head: Memorandum From the President’s Assistant for National Security Affairs (McFarlane) to President Reagan

list.label: SUBJECT
list.item: Secretary Shultz’ visit to Venezuela, Brazil and El Salvador

div.p: Venezuela will inaugurate its sixth consecutive democratically elected President Jaime Lusinchi on February 3, 1984, and Secretary Shultz suggests that he lead the delegation and then continue on to visit Brazil and El Salvador.

Dr. Lusinchi and his Social Democratic Party won the Venezuelan elections by a large margin and want to establish a close working relationship with us. The President-elect has told us that Venezuela will continue to stress the importance of democracy in Central America as part of the Contadora negotiating process. Venezuela must also reschedule its $35 billion foreign debt and cope with severe economic problems triggered by the fall in price of its major export, oil.

In Brazil, Secretary Shultz wants to demonstrate symbolic support to follow-up on your visit of last year and to assist both the continuation of the democratization process and the orderly resolution of its economic problems—especially the continuing refinancing of its $90 billion foreign debt.
In El Salvador, Secretary Shultz wants to follow-up the Vice President’s successful visit of December 11, and have a regional strategy meeting with U.S. Ambassadors from the area.

The just-elected Social Democratic Party of Venezuela has two factions—one led by the President-elect with a strong labor union base which is realistic about the communist threat in
Central America, and a second group, led by former President Carlos Andres Perez, which has been naive in expecting positive results from coalitions with the communists in Central America. It is very important that the U.S. provide the new President-elect with timely information and support so that his group will shape Venezuela’s foreign policy in the Caribbean region in a constructive way. Secretary Shultz’s visit can be an important part of that process. His visit to Brazil and El Salvador—delayed by the October tragedy in Lebanon and our rescue mission in Grenada—also can make a positive contribution.
That you approve the request of Secretary Shultz to visit Venezuela, Brazil and El Salvador in February 1984.

note.p: Secret. Sent for action. Copies were sent to Bush, Meese, Baker, Deaver, and Herrington. A stamped notation at the top of the page indicates that Reagan saw the memorandum. Reagan also wrote his initials at the top of the page.

In telegram 10935 from Caracas, December 15, the Embassy reported on Stone’s December 13 meeting with Lusinchi who “said his government would place a high priority on Central America and would take a more vigorous and authentic role in the currently stalled Contadora process.” Referring to El Salvador, Lusinchi “said that regimes that negate democracy cannot be accepted.” (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D830741–0196)
Reagan indicated his approval by drawing a check mark and signing his initials.
